name: microstructure_reversion_5s
author: adapted from claude-4.6-opus
thesis: Inferred order flow imbalance — approximated from volume on up-bars vs down-bars over a short rolling window — can detect when aggressive buying or selling has temporarily exhausted available liquidity. When buy-volume imbalance exceeds 70% of total volume over the last 10 bars but price stops advancing, it signals that buying pressure has been absorbed by limit sellers (institutional supply). The resulting reversion occurs as the aggressive buyers have been filled and new buying flow dries up. The edge exists because order flow imbalance analysis is typically done with L2 data which retail traders rarely have; this approximation using 1-min bar data provides a noisy but usable signal. The edge persists because the signal is inherently noisy and requires calibration — most retail traders give up after initial false signals.
mechanism: Order flow imbalance between aggressive buyers and sellers creates short-term price pressure. When buy-side aggression exceeds sell-side by a threshold, the order book tilts and market makers adjust their quotes upward. This creates a 15-45 second drift before the book rebalances as new limit orders arrive to capture the improved price.

exit.signal_exit: exit if imbalance deepens (buy_imbalance > 0.80 for shorts, < 0.20 for longs)

filters.vix_filter: none — flow imbalance works across vol regimes
filters.volume_filter: need sufficient volume for buy/sell split to be meaningful: > 0.8x SMA(volume, 20)

weaknesses: Buy/sell volume split from bar OHLCV is a crude approximation — true order flow requires tick-level or L2 data
The 10-bar window is arbitrary and likely not optimal across all stocks; needs per-stock calibration
In low-tick-count environments (illiquid stocks), the buy/sell volume approximation breaks down completely
prior_art: Order flow imbalance research: Cont et al. (2014) 'Price Impact of Order Flow Imbalances'. Buy/sell volume approximation from OHLCV: known as the 'close location value' or CLV (Chaiken). Accumulation/Distribution line by Chaikin uses similar logic. The 10-bar rolling imbalance approach is closer to the VPIN concept (Easley et al., 2012).
adaptation_notes: Converted from 1min to 5s bars. Lookback multiplier: 12x. Adaptations: timeframe scaling to 5-second candles; signal conversion from individual stock to NIFTY/BANKNIFTY index; lookback period scaling for 5-second bars; stop/target recalibration for 5-second timeframe. Stop/target calibrated for options point-based exits. Universe narrowed to NIFTY index.
